q: Most viruses have a size in the range of about:
x: Viruses are roughly 20–300 nm across, far smaller than bacteria (about 1–10 µm). This is why most can only be seen with an electron microscope.

q: The approximate diameter of a human immunodeficiency virus particle is:
x: HIV is a roughly spherical enveloped virus about 100 nm in diameter. 1 µm and 10 µm are the sizes of bacteria and body cells.

q: Among the following, the largest and most complex animal viruses are the:
x: Poxviruses (such as the smallpox virus) are large brick-shaped viruses, about 250–300 nm long. Polio-, parvo- and rhinoviruses are small icosahedral viruses.

q: Inside the HIV capsid, the viral enzyme protease is needed to:
o: Copy the viral RNA into DNA
Insert viral DNA into the host chromosome
Cut large viral polyproteins into functional proteins so new virions mature
Attach the virus to the CD4 receptor
x: Protease cleaves long viral polyproteins into working capsid proteins and enzymes, letting new particles mature. Copying RNA into DNA is the job of reverse transcriptase, and insertion is done by integrase.

q: An icosahedral (polyhedral) capsid is a solid made of:
x: An icosahedron has 20 equilateral triangular faces and 12 corners. Many viruses, such as adenovirus and poliovirus, have this capsid shape.

q: The HIV envelope glycoprotein gp41 mainly helps the virus to:
o: Bind first to the CD4 receptor
Fuse its envelope with the membrane of the host cell
Leave the host cell by lysis
x: gp41 is the transmembrane glycoprotein that anchors gp120 and brings about fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane. The first binding to CD4 is done by gp120.

q: Which of the following viruses has a polyhedral (icosahedral) capsid?
x: Adenovirus has a regular icosahedral capsid. Tobacco mosaic virus is helical, T4 is complex (head plus tail) and rabies virus is bullet-shaped.

q: Passage of HIV from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy, birth or breast-feeding is called:
x: Transmission from mother to child is called vertical transmission. Spread between unrelated people, for example by sex or shared needles, is horizontal transmission.

q: Besides protecting the nucleic acid, the capsid of a naked virus also:
o: Helps the virus attach to receptors on the host cell
Carries out respiration for the virus
x: The capsid shields the genome and, in non-enveloped viruses, carries the proteins that bind host receptors. Viruses have no metabolism, so they make no ATP and no proteins on their own.

q: HIV is NOT spread by mosquito bites mainly because:
o: The virus does not multiply in the mosquito, and the mosquito injects saliva, not earlier blood
Mosquitoes never bite people infected with HIV
HIV is killed by the heat of the human body
Mosquito saliva contains antibodies against HIV
x: HIV cannot replicate in insect cells, and when a mosquito feeds it injects only its saliva, not blood from a previous person. So the insect does not act as a vector.

q: Which of the following viruses is naked, that is, it has no lipid envelope?
x: Poliovirus consists only of an icosahedral protein capsid around its RNA. Influenza virus, HIV and herpes virus all carry an envelope taken from host membranes.

q: Outside the body HIV survives poorly. It is readily destroyed by:
o: Exposure to normal room air for a few seconds only
x: HIV's lipid envelope is fragile, so heat, drying and disinfectants such as bleach inactivate it. Antibiotics act on bacteria and have no effect on viruses.

q: The glycoprotein spikes, such as haemagglutinin, on the envelope of the influenza virus mainly help the virus to:
o: Attach to specific receptors on host cells
x: Envelope spikes are the attachment proteins: haemagglutinin binds receptors on cells of the respiratory tract. The genome is inside the capsid, and viruses make no ATP.

q: A few weeks after infection with HIV, many people develop:
o: No change at all at any stage
A short flu-like illness with fever, sore throat and rash
x: The acute stage of HIV infection, 2–4 weeks after exposure, often causes a brief flu-like illness. Opportunistic infections appear years later, when helper T cells have fallen very low.

q: The genetic material of poliovirus is:
x: Poliovirus is a small naked RNA virus with a single strand of RNA. Double-stranded DNA is found in viruses such as herpes, adeno- and poxviruses.

q: An HIV-infected person is diagnosed as having AIDS when the helper T (CD4) cell count falls below about:
x: A normal CD4 count is roughly 500–1500 cells per mm³. When it falls below about 200 per mm³, immunity is so weak that AIDS is diagnosed.

q: Which group contains only DNA viruses?
o: Influenza virus, measles virus and poliovirus
Rabies virus, mumps virus and HIV
Tobacco mosaic virus, rotavirus and dengue virus
x: Herpes-, adeno- and poxviruses all have double-stranded DNA. Every virus in the other groups has RNA as its genetic material.

q: In many developing countries, including Pakistan, the most common serious bacterial opportunistic infection in people with AIDS is:
x: Weak cell-mediated immunity lets Mycobacterium tuberculosis become active, so tuberculosis is the leading opportunistic infection in AIDS patients in such countries.

q: Most plant viruses contain RNA. An exception that has double-stranded DNA is:
x: Cauliflower mosaic virus is a well-known plant virus with double-stranded DNA. Tobacco mosaic virus and potato virus X are RNA viruses, and cotton leaf curl virus has single-stranded DNA.

q: White patches of oral thrush in the mouth of an AIDS patient are caused by:
x: Oral thrush is an opportunistic infection by the yeast-like fungus Candida, which grows freely when cell-mediated immunity fails.

q: Dengue fever, a viral disease common in Pakistan, is spread from person to person by:
x: Dengue virus is carried by Aedes mosquitoes, mainly Aedes aegypti. Anopheles mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite, which is a protozoan, not a virus.

q: AIDS was first recognised as a new disease in the year:
x: AIDS was first described in the USA in 1981; HIV was identified as its cause shortly afterwards.

q: Hepatitis C, which is common in Pakistan, spreads mainly through:
o: Contaminated blood, for example reused syringes
Food and water contaminated with faeces
x: The hepatitis C virus is blood-borne, as is the hepatitis B virus, so reused syringes, unscreened blood and unsterile instruments spread it. Faecally contaminated food and water spread other hepatitis viruses instead.

q: Among injecting drug users, the most direct way to prevent the spread of HIV is to:
o: Use a new sterile syringe and needle for every injection
Inject only into muscles, not veins
Wash the syringe with cold water between users
x: HIV passes in traces of blood left in shared needles and syringes, so a fresh sterile set for each injection stops this route. Antibiotics do not act on viruses, and cold-water rinsing does not remove infected blood.

q: Poliovirus enters the body through the mouth and causes paralysis by destroying:
o: Red blood cells in the liver
Motor neurons in the spinal cord
Cells lining the air sacs of the lungs
x: Poliovirus spreads by the faecal–oral route and can invade the nervous system, killing motor neurons of the spinal cord so that muscles become paralysed.

q: A positive ELISA result for HIV antibodies is usually confirmed by a more specific test called the:
x: ELISA is a sensitive screening test; a positive result is confirmed by the Western blot. The Widal test is for typhoid and the Mantoux test is for tuberculosis.

q: A child has high fever, cough, red eyes and a red rash spreading over the body. The disease is caught by breathing in droplets. The most likely viral disease is:
x: Measles spreads through respiratory droplets and causes fever, cough and a typical red skin rash. Polio causes paralysis, rabies attacks nerves after a bite, and hepatitis A affects the liver.

q: Which combination of features correctly describes HIV?
o: Enveloped virus with single-stranded DNA and no enzymes
Naked virus with RNA and a protein tail
Enveloped virus with RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase
x: HIV has a lipid envelope with glycoprotein spikes, an RNA genome and carries reverse transcriptase, which makes it a retrovirus.

q: The common cold is most often caused by:
x: Rhinoviruses infect the lining of the nose and are the commonest cause of the common cold. Rotaviruses cause diarrhoea in children.

q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of AIDS?
o: Diarrhoea lasting more than a month
A steady rise in the number of helper T cells
x: In AIDS helper T cells fall, they do not rise. Chronic diarrhoea, night sweats, fever and weight loss are all typical signs.

q: Viruses such as rabies virus and poliovirus, which mainly attack the nervous system, are described as:
x: Classified by the tissue they attack, viruses that target nerves are neurotropic. Dermotropic viruses attack the skin, pneumotropic the lungs, and viscerotropic the internal organs such as the liver.

q: Antiretroviral drugs can lower HIV in the blood to very low levels, yet the infection cannot be cured. The main reason is that:
o: HIV is a bacterium resistant to all drugs
Viral DNA integrated in long-lived host cells stays hidden and inactive
The drugs destroy all helper T cells
HIV can live freely outside cells for years
x: As a provirus, HIV DNA sits silently inside the chromosomes of resting cells, where drugs and the immune system cannot reach it. When treatment stops, these cells can start making virus again.

q: Bacteriophage lambda can either destroy its host or join its DNA to the bacterial chromosome. It is therefore an example of a:
x: A phage that can enter the lysogenic cycle is temperate; lambda is the standard example. A virulent phage such as T4 always follows the lytic cycle.

q: Doctors treat HIV with a combination of three or more different drugs instead of one drug. The main reason is that:
o: One drug alone kills too many helper T cells
Each drug works only on one organ
Combined drugs make the virus leave the body in urine
HIV mutates quickly, and several drugs together make drug-resistant virus far less likely
x: Because HIV makes many copying errors, a single drug soon selects resistant mutants. A virus would need several mutations at once to escape a combination, so resistance develops much more slowly.

q: The genetic material of bacteriophage T4 is:
x: T4 has a linear double-stranded DNA molecule packed in its polyhedral head, which it injects into the bacterium.

q: Worldwide, the most common way in which HIV is passed from one adult to another is:
x: Most adult HIV infections are acquired through unprotected sex. HIV is not spread by casual contact, droplets or insects.

q: The three basic types of capsid symmetry in viruses are:
x: Capsids are helical (such as TMV), icosahedral or polyhedral (such as adenovirus), or complex (such as bacteriophage T4). Coccus, bacillus and spirillum are shapes of bacteria.

q: HIV shows a very high rate of mutation mainly because its reverse transcriptase:
o: Is produced by the host's B cells
Works only in the presence of antibiotics
Makes many errors and does not correct them while copying RNA into DNA
x: Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, so many mistakes enter each new copy of the genome. This produces many variants of HIV within one person.

q: Influenza virus carries its genes as:
o: Several separate segments of single-stranded RNA
One circular molecule of double-stranded DNA
One long molecule of double-stranded RNA
x: Influenza virus has a segmented genome: eight separate pieces of single-stranded RNA. Mixing of segments between strains helps produce new flu strains.

q: A baby born to an HIV-positive mother tests positive for HIV antibodies at birth, though the baby may not be infected. This is because:
o: The baby has already made antibodies in the womb in every case
HIV antibodies are inherited through the mother's genes
Antibodies from the mother cross the placenta into the baby's blood
The test always gives a false result in newborns
x: Maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and stay in the baby's blood for many months, so an antibody test cannot tell whether the baby itself is infected.

q: The capsid of a virus together with the nucleic acid enclosed in it is called the:
x: Capsid plus genome is the nucleocapsid. A capsomere is a single protein subunit of the capsid, and the envelope is the outer lipid layer of some viruses.

q: A nurse is accidentally pricked by a needle just used on an HIV-positive patient. This is an example of HIV exposure through:
x: A needle-stick injury carries a small amount of infected blood directly into the body. HIV is not spread by air, food or saliva on intact skin.

q: Cotton leaf curl virus is carried from one cotton plant to another mainly by:
x: Cotton leaf curl virus is transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) as it feeds on the phloem sap; controlling whiteflies reduces the disease.

q: An opportunistic infection is one that:
o: Affects only people who travel abroad
Is always caused by HIV itself
Is caused by microbes that rarely harm people with a healthy immune system
x: Opportunistic microbes are normally kept in check by the immune system; they cause disease when immunity is weak, as in AIDS.

q: Viruses are said to lie on the borderline of living and non-living. A feature that links them with living organisms is that they:
o: Have no metabolism of their own
x: Having genetic material that is inherited and can mutate is a feature of life. Crystallisation and lack of metabolism are features of non-living things.

q: Which of the following is NOT a measure that helps reduce the spread of HIV?
x: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so they do not prevent HIV. Blood screening, sterile syringes and safe sexual behaviour all block known routes of spread.

q: Under the electron microscope, rabies virus is seen to have a shape described as:
x: Rabies virus is an enveloped helical RNA virus with a characteristic bullet shape. Poxviruses are brick-shaped and bacteriophages are tadpole-like.
